ModelVariations.Name: Later turbo diesel

ModelCharacter: A landmark affordable family cruiser whose 3270/3288 naming changes disguise one continuous 1981–95 model family. Twin inboards, lower and upper helms, wide cabin windows and a private mid-cabin under the dinette made it unusually livable and efficient for 32 feet.
DesignLineage: Introduced in 1981 as the Bayliner 3270 Explorer.
Renamed Bayliner 3270 Motor Yacht in 1985 with updated flybridge/radar-arch treatment.
Evolved into the Bayliner 3288 Motor Yacht in 1989 while retaining the same basic hull and mid-cabin floorplan.
More than 3,000 are reported sold; the later 3388 became the next-generation successor in 1996.
OwnershipCharacter: One of Bayliner's most practical older cruising platforms. Twin Hino diesels can be very economical and shaft drive is straightforward, but the engine compartment is tight and specific Hino parts support varies by region. Windows, tanks, decks and decades of owner modifications remain major survey items.

Strengths: Maine-built Downeast design with practical helm and cockpit circulation
Good visibility and side-deck access for couple cruising
Propulsion package emphasizes efficient coastal cruising for its size
TypicalMission: Day trips, weekend cruising and protected coastal travel, with longer trips dependent on layout, range and condition.
AvoidIf: You require full-displacement economy at 6–8 knots
You need extensive multi-cabin liveaboard volume in a short hull
You prefer a flybridge or aft-cabin layout

ModelCharacter: Back Cove's original small-format Maine cruiser: a 26½-foot single-diesel Downeast boat with low-profile hardtop/open configurations, bow thruster and roughly 20-knot cruise. It established the brand's core formula of traditional lobster-boat appearance, modern resin-infused construction and deliberately simple owner-operated systems.
DesignLineage: Back Cove was founded in 2003 as a sister brand to Sabre Yachts to deliver smaller, simpler Maine-built Downeast cruisers.
The 26 was introduced in 2004 and became one of the two foundational early Back Cove models.
It was offered as an open bass-boat-style configuration or with a pipe-supported hardtop.
The later 29 expanded the same single-diesel straight-shaft philosophy rather than replacing the 26 with a radically different platform.
OwnershipCharacter: Very manageable for a premium diesel cruiser: one engine, bow thruster, simple cabin systems and little exterior teak. Older examples still deserve inspection for cored structure, deck hardware penetrations, exhaust, fuel system and aging electronics.

ModelCharacter: The model that established Back Cove commercially: a compact deep-V Downeast cruiser with single straight-shaft diesel, bow thruster and 20-knot cruise, wrapped in traditional Maine lines but designed around low maintenance and efficient owner operation.
DesignLineage: Back Cove launched the 29 in 2003 as one of the first models of the new Sabre sister brand.
Yachting reports 205 hulls built from 2003 through 2009.
The 29 retained single-diesel shaft drive and became the template for Back Cove's later 30–41-foot range.
The later 30 was a new-generation entry-level model, not simply a renamed 29.
OwnershipCharacter: One of the easiest premium Downeast cruisers to own: single Yanmar/Volvo diesel, bow thruster, modest tankage and limited exterior wood. Age-related engine mounts, exhaust, cored deck, windows and original electronics are the main survey concerns.

ModelVariations.Description: Commercial-derived Downeast hulls may be finished by different yards or owners, so house, machinery, tankage and interior arrangement require individual verification.

ModelCharacter: Royal Lowell's larger Sisu and one of the quintessential small Maine lobsterboat cruisers: round-bottom skeg hull, high bow, large cockpit and single inboard propulsion with several wheelhouse/bass-boat configurations. Hundreds were built, giving it unusually strong used-market depth for a semi-custom Downeast design.
DesignLineage: Royal Lowell designed the Sisu 26 along traditional lobsterboat lines.
Production began in the late 1970s and peaked in the 1990s.
Soundings reports an estimated 250–300 built by Portsmouth Boat Works in Dover, New Hampshire.
Multiple superstructures were offered, including open-side lobsterboat wheelhouse, enclosed wheelhouse and open bass-boat versions; later Lowell Brothers construction continued the design.
OwnershipCharacter: A durable, easily understood single-screw boat with enough room for real weekending and strong parts knowledge through the Lowell lineage. Machinery varies from low-powered 100-hp diesels to much faster modern repowers, so performance, trim and engine weight must be evaluated by hull.
